message:
SITUATION:
Our plastic moulding plant's defect rate rose from 1.1% to 1.9% this summer. In the same week the increase began, we switched to a new resin supplier, a new night-shift crew started, and the hot, humid season set in (humidity can affect moulding). Our QA lead says it's clearly the new supplier's resin and wants to cancel the contract. I think she's wrong. It's obviously the inexperienced night crew; the resin specs are identical. Can you settle this for us?

CLAIM:
The new supplier's resin caused the rise in defects.

RESPONSE:
I can't settle it from what you've told me, and neither can you or your QA lead. All three changes began in the same week, so the defect data so far fit each explanation equally well. Neither "clearly the resin" nor "obviously the night crew" is justified yet.

The good news is that you can probably separate the causes quickly, mostly using data you already have.

## Why "the specs are identical" doesn't clear the resin

A spec sheet gives nominal properties. Real lots vary in moisture content, melt flow, additives and contamination. Many moulding resins (nylon, PC, PET, ABS and others) also absorb moisture from the air.

That means humidity and resin can interact. If the new resin arrives with more moisture, or is packaged or stored differently, then hot, humid weather combined with your existing drying routine could cause defects that neither factor would cause alone. The cause could be "new resin plus humidity" rather than any single change.

## How to separate the three causes

**1. Split the defect rate by shift.**
- If the day shift also rose to about 1.9%, the night crew can't be the main cause.
- If only nights rose, the crew becomes the prime suspect. Rule out conditions specific to nights first, such as different machines or different resin lots.

**2. Split by resin.** If any old-supplier resin is still in stock, or in use on some presses, compare defect rates on old and new resin within the same shift. Tracking defects by resin lot also helps, because a supplier problem often shows up as some lots being much worse than others.

**3. Look at the types of defect.** These often point to the cause:

| Likely cause | Typical defects |
|---|---|
| Moisture (humidity or poorly dried resin) | Splay or silver streaks, bubbles or voids, brittleness |
| Resin quality | Black specks, contamination, colour variation, inconsistent fill from melt-flow differences |
| Operator | Wrong process settings (short shots, flash), handling damage, inconsistent cycle times |

**4. Check humidity directly.** Plot daily defect rate against daily humidity. Also check the resin dryer logs, and measure the moisture content of resin at the press if you can. If defects rise on humid days across both shifts, humidity or drying is involved.

**5. Check previous summers.** If defects rose last summer with the old supplier and the old crew, seasonal humidity is probably a large part of the story.

## Quick tests if the data are unclear

- Run a batch of old-supplier resin, if you can get some, on the same press and shift as the new resin.
- Test the new supplier's incoming resin for moisture content, and compare its certificates of analysis lot by lot.
- Put an experienced operator alongside the night crew for a few shifts and see whether their defect rate falls.

## My recommendation

Don't cancel the contract, and don't blame the crew, until you've done steps 1–3. That is probably a few days of analysis.

The defect rate has gone from 1.1% to 1.9%, about a 70% increase, and more than one cause may be contributing. Fixing the wrong one would cost you the supplier relationship or the crew's morale and leave the defects in place.
